1.title: Managing a Stage Boundary in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Managing a Stage Boundary in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two processes. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. four point six.one apply managing a stage boundary: activities, inputs and outputs, roles and responsibilities, how the practices are applied. four point six.two analyze whether the activities, roles and responsibilities are effective and fit for purpose, considering tailoring, the practices, and the purpose and objectives of the process. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two processes (thirty percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Managing a stage boundary is the process the project manager uses near the end of a stage so the board can decide about the next one. The figure shows the flow.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. The figure shows this: Managing a stage boundary: the project manager reports the stage end, updates the business case and project plan, plans the next stage and asks the board to decide.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Purpose: give the board enough information to review the success of the current stage, approve the next stage plan, review the updated project plan and confirm continued business justification and acceptable risk. Objectives: the board is assured that the stage's products are complete and approved; the next stage plan, project plan and business case are updated; lessons are recorded; authorization for the next stage is requested. The process is also used when the board asks for an exception plan. It is not used at the end of the last stage, which closing a project handles.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Manage by stages. Each stage ends with a board decision before the next begins. Continued business justification. The business case is refreshed and re-checked. Manage by exception. An exception plan replaces a plan that would be exceeded. Focus on products. The report shows which products were completed and approved. Exam tip: Stage boundary means: review this stage, plan the next, confirm the business case, and the board decides. The project manager never authorizes the next stage.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. The names below give the general idea; check the Official Book's wording for the activities. Plan the next stage. Prepares the next stage plan in detail, with products, resources, tolerances and risks. Update the project plan. Adds actuals and approved changes, and re-forecasts the remaining stages. Update the business case. Refreshes costs, benefits and risks, and checks the project is still justified.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Report stage end. Writes the end stage report: performance against the plan, products approved, issues, risks, lessons. Produce an exception plan. When the board asks after an exception, replaces the plan that would be exceeded.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Inputs. The current stage plan and actuals; the project plan; the business case; product approvals; the project log; the board's request for an exception plan. Outputs. End stage report; next stage plan or exception plan; updated project plan and business case; updated risk register; lessons; a request to authorize the next stage. Exam tip: An exception plan replaces the plan that will be exceeded, and the board asks for it. A stage plan covers the next stage only.

1.title: Roles
1.text: Roles. Project manager. Responsible: prepares the report, plans and updates; asks the board to decide. Team managers. Give estimates and detail for the next stage's work. Executive. Owns the business case and checks it still justifies the project. Senior user. Confirms user needs and expected benefits still hold. Senior supplier. Confirms the supplier can deliver the next stage plan. Project board. Reviews the information and decides, in directing a project. Project assurance. Reviews the report, plans and business case independently. Project support. Collects actuals, updates registers, assembles documents. Check the book's roles table. If a plan would breach the project tolerances, the board goes to the corporate or programme level.

1.title: How the practices are applied
1.text: How the practices are applied. Business case. Update costs and benefits; check benefits are still expected and justified. Organization. Check the team and roles still suit the next stage. Plans. Next stage plan in detail; project plan updated; exception plan if asked. Quality. Confirm products are approved; set quality needs for the next stage. Risk. Re-assess risks and exposure; update the risk register. Issues. Review open issues; carry forward or close them. Progress. End stage report; tolerances for the next stage; lessons.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. The report compares actuals with the plan and gives the board enough to decide. A bulky or thin report, or one sent for information only. Business case, benefits and risks re-checked with current figures. Business case left as it was at initiation. Next stage planned in detail, later stages in outline. All remaining stages planned in detail, or no next stage plan.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Project plan updated for the effect on later stages. Project plan unchanged, or tolerance quietly extended. Exception plan produced when the board asks. A new stage plan used to hide an overspend. The board decides before the next stage starts. The next stage starts before authorization. Lessons used in the next stage plan. Lessons ignored.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring changes the form, not the decision. Stage lengths: shorter stages give more control where risk or uncertainty is high; longer ones suit stable work. A project needs at least two management stages. Management and technical stages: a management stage is a board control point. A technical stage groups work by skill or product type, such as design or build, and can overlap others. A technical stage ending is not a board decision point. Small projects: a short report and one meeting, with decisions recorded.

2.title: Judging a scenario, continued
2.text: Judging a scenario. Agile or incremental delivery: align a boundary with a release and replan from what was delivered. Sustainability, digital and data: re-check sustainability measures and data risks. Exam tip: Board decisions belong to management stages, not technical stages. Do not add a formal board gate each time a technical stage finishes.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. The build stage of Project Harbor ends in two weeks. To save time, Sam Okafor asks Delta Software to start the pilot stage before the board has reviewed the end stage report. Was this an appropriate action for the project manager to take, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: No, because only the board can authorize the next stage to start. The board authorizes each stage in directing a project, so work on the next stage waits for its decision (manage by stages).

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. At the end of the pilot stage, Project Harbor's business case still shows the costs and permit fees from initiation. Delta Software has since raised its price, and fewer berths will use the service. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Update the business case and send it with the end stage report. The stage boundary refreshes the business case so the board can confirm continued justification.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. After an exception report, the board asks Sam Okafor for an exception plan. Sam writes one that replaces the rest of the current stage plan, starts from the actuals to date, and shows the revised cost, end date and effect on the business case. Was this an appropriate action, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because an exception plan replaces the plan being exceeded. An exception plan replaces the plan that would be exceeded, starts from the actuals and shows the board the effect.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Sam Okafor has sent the board the end stage report and the next stage plan for the pilot stage. Project tolerances are not forecast to be exceeded. Who decides whether the pilot stage can start? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The project board as a group. The project board authorizes each stage, and corporate management is involved only if project tolerances would be exceeded.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Before deciding on the pilot stage, the board of Project Harbor wants to see how the build stage performed against its plan, which products were approved and what was learned. Which management product gives this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: End stage report. The end stage report reviews the stage that is ending; the end project report covers the whole project only at closure.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Delta Software's design work, a technical stage, finishes in week eight of the twelve-week build stage. Sam asks the board for a formal stage boundary decision at that point. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: No, because the board decides at management stages, not technical ones. The board's control points are management stages, and a technical stage grouping work by skill is not one.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the purpose of managing a stage boundary? Answer: To give the board enough information to review the stage, approve the next stage plan and confirm continued business justification. Question two. When is managing a stage boundary not used? Answer: At the end of the last stage, which uses closing a project. Question three. Name the five activities. Answer: Plan the next stage, update the project plan, update the business case, report stage end and produce an exception plan.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is an exception plan? Answer: A plan that replaces the one that would be exceeded, produced when the board asks for it. Question five. Name two outputs of the process. Answer: The end stage report and the next stage plan. Question six. What is a technical stage? Answer: A grouping of work by skill or product type, not a board decision point.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Purpose: board reviews the stage, approves the next stage plan, confirms the business case. When: near the end of every stage except the last. Activities: plan the next stage, update plan and business case, report stage end, exception plan. Outputs: end stage report, next stage plan, updated plan and business case, lessons. Effective: enough information, benefits and risks re-checked, decision first. Red flags: stale business case, next stage starts early, exception hidden in a stage plan. Tailoring: stage length, management versus technical stage, lighter reports.
